extracted.intended_audience: practitioners before the USPTO (patent attorneys/agents), USPTO OED counsel, and administrative law judges handling USPTO discipline
extracted.subtask_description: Standards, legal tests, and regulatory provisions applied in USPTO Office of Enrollment and Discipline proceedings (summary judgment, collateral estoppel, specified Disciplinary Rules, and sanctions analysis). Useful for evaluating practitioner misconduct and appropriate sanctions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Summary judgment standard
rubrics_metrics.description: Summary judgment is proper where no genuine issue of material fact exists and the moving party is entitled to judgment as a matter of law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The moving party bears a heavy burden of demonstrating the absence of any material issues of fact. All ambiguities and reasonable inferences must be drawn in favor of the non-moving party. A fact is not 'material' unless it will affect the outcome of the proceeding. Case citations: Anderson v. Liberty Lobby, Inc., Celotex Corp. v. Catrett, Matsushita Elec. Indus. Corp. v. Zenith Radio Corp.; see also Fed. R. Civ. P. 56(c). Summary judgment is a 'drastic device.' If the record, taken as a whole, could not lead a reasonable trier of fact to find for the non-moving party, there is no genuine issue for trial.

rubrics_metrics.name: Collateral estoppel (under Texas law)
rubrics_metrics.description: A party seeking to assert collateral estoppel must establish that (1) the facts sought to be litigated in the second action were fully and fairly litigated in the first action; (2) those facts were essential to the judgment in the first action; and (3) the parties were cast as adversaries in the first action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Federal courts must give state judgments the preclusive effect the state would give (28 U.S.C. § 1738). Texas law treats default judgments as capable of having preclusive effect: actual litigation focuses on what was actually litigated and determined, not what could have been. Examples and supporting authorities: Van Dyke v. Boswell; Mendez v. Haynes Brinkley & Co.; Fullerton (5th Cir.). Default judgments may be 'full and fair' where issues were pled and determined even if unopposed.

rubrics_metrics.name: 37 C.F.R. § 10.23(a) — disreputable or gross misconduct
rubrics_metrics.description: Regulation states that a practitioner 'shall not engage in disreputable or gross misconduct.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applied to conduct such as failing to perform retained legal services, falsely representing that work was performed (e.g., that patent applications were filed when they were not), and accepting payment for services not performed. Violations of this provision may be established by undisputed facts (e.g., state court default judgment and other evidence).

rubrics_metrics.name: 37 C.F.R. § 10.23(b)(4) — dishonesty, fraud, deceit, or misrepresentation
rubrics_metrics.description: A practitioner shall not 'engage in conduct involving dishonesty, fraud, deceit, or misrepresentation.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include representing (in invoices or emails) that patent applications were prepared and filed when they were not, and sending invoices/accepting payments for work not performed. Such conduct supports finding violations of this rule.

rubrics_metrics.name: 37 C.F.R. § 10.23(b)(6) — catch-all adverse-reflection provision
rubrics_metrics.description: Prohibits 'engaging in any other conduct that adversely reflects on the practitioner's fitness to practice before the Office.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a residual catch-all intended to reach misconduct not already covered by other rules. It should not be used to duplicate conduct already encompassed by other specific Disciplinary Rules; the OED Director must allege 'other conduct' beyond what's covered elsewhere to sustain a § 10.23(b)(6) violation.

rubrics_metrics.name: 37 C.F.R. § 10.23(c)(3) — misappropriation/failure to remit funds
rubrics_metrics.description: Conduct that constitutes a violation includes '[m]isappropriation of, or failure to properly or timely remit, funds received by a practitioner ... from a client to pay a fee which the client is required by law to pay to the Office.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Accepting payments (including fees purportedly for filing) and failing to file the related applications can constitute a violation. The rule applies where fees required to be paid to the Office are not properly remitted because the practitioner did not perform the filing or remit the funds.

rubrics_metrics.name: 37 C.F.R. § 10.77(c) — neglect of legal matter
rubrics_metrics.description: A practitioner shall not '[n]eglect a legal matter entrusted to the practitioner.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Failing to prepare and file patent applications for which the practitioner was engaged constitutes neglect under this rule.

rubrics_metrics.name: 37 C.F.R. § 10.84(a) — failure to seek lawful objectives/perform contract
rubrics_metrics.description: A practitioner shall not intentionally '[f]ail to seek the lawful objectives of a client through reasonably available means permitted by law and the Disciplinary Rules ... fail to carry out a contract of employment entered into with a client for professional services ... or prejudice or damage a client during the course of a professional relationship.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Failing to perform contracted-for services (preparing/filing applications) and invoicing for services not provided are violations. This rule captures the obligation to carry out professional engagements and the harm caused by breach.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sanctions analysis — four-factor test (37 C.F.R. § 11.54(b))
rubrics_metrics.description: Before imposing suspension or exclusion, consider: (1) did the practitioner violate a duty owed to a client/public/legal system/profession? (2) did the practitioner act intentionally, knowingly, or negligently? (3) what amount of actual or potential injury was caused? (4) are there aggravating or mitigating factors?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply each factor to the undisputed facts. Examples from the decision: (1) duty violation shown by failing to perform contracted services and misrepresenting work; (2) knowing/intentional conduct inferred from accepting payment despite not filing; (3) injury measured by money paid ($35,225) and potential loss of patent rights; (4) aggravating factors include repeated conduct, deception, refusal to return files/payment, failure to participate in proceedings, lack of explanation or mitigation (e.g., no evidence of incapacity). The combined analysis can support exclusion from practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Application of default judgments as preclusive evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Default judgments may operate as preclusive findings of fact for later proceedings if they were 'intended in all respects as final and appealable' and the defendant had the opportunity to contest but did not.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When a defendant fails to appear and a default judgment issues, the judgment's implicit findings (e.g., that contracted work was not performed) may be used offensively to bar relitigation. Courts look to whether the issue was actually raised and determined; prior decisions (Van Dyke, Mendez, Fullerton) support preclusive effect of defaults in Texas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limits on using § 10.23(b)(6) where other rules apply
rubrics_metrics.description: The catch-all § 10.23(b)(6) cannot be used to punish conduct already encompassed by other Disciplinary Rules without alleging 'other conduct' beyond those rules.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the alleged misconduct is covered by specific rules (e.g., § 10.23(a), (b)(4), (c)(3), § 10.77, § 10.84), a violation of § 10.23(b)(6) should not be found absent distinct additional misconduct. The decision denied summary judgment on Count 10 alleging § 10.23(b)(6) because the OED Director did not allege conduct beyond what other rules already covered.

rubrics_metrics.name: Procedural appellate timeline and service requirements (37 C.F.R. § 11.55 and § 11.54)
rubrics_metrics.description: Appeals from an Initial Decision to the USPTO Director must be filed within 30 days; cross-appeals, appellee briefs, appellee/cross-appellee reply briefs have set deadlines; finality occurs in absence of appeal per 37 C.F.R. § 11.54.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The decision lists specific time limits: appeal within 30 days, cross-appeal by later of 14 days after service of appeal or 30 days after Initial Decision; appellee or cross-appellee briefs within 30 days after service; reply briefs within 14 days after service. Briefs filed with USPTO Director and copies served on opposing parties and HUD Office of Hearings and Appeals. Final decision becomes final 30 days from Initial Decision if no appeal (37 C.F.R. § 11.54).
